title: Encoding in Long-Term Memory
summary: How we file experiences into long-term memory through association and organisation, what tip-of-the-tongue states reveal, and the dual-coding hypothesis.

lesson.title: Filing memories so you can find them
lesson.hook: You can remember your last birthday by thinking of the cake, the friends, the song or the rain that day. Why do so many different doors lead to the same memory?

slides.heading: Many roads to one memory
slides.body:
**Encoding** is how information is put into memory in a form we can later find. Long-term memory works less like a box and more like a **library catalogue**: each memory is filed under many 'index cards'.

A picnic at Millennium Park in Abuja could be reached through 'parks', 'friends', 'jollof rice' or 'mosquito bites'. The **more associations** a memory has, the easier it is to retrieve.

slides.heading: Highlights, not recordings
slides.body:
Memory does not store **every detail**. After three hours at a picnic, you will not remember every word spoken or every face seen. You keep the **highlights**: the gist and the moments that mattered.

This is efficient, not faulty. Encoding is selective, shaped by attention and by what makes sense to you.

slides.heading: Rehearsal is a continuum
slides.body:
At one end is **rote rehearsal**: simple repetition, like chanting a formula. It can get information into long-term memory, but weakly.

At the other end is **elaborative rehearsal**, also called **association rehearsal**: linking new information to what you **already know**. The more connections you build, the stronger the encoding. Craik and Lockhart's (1972) levels-of-processing idea makes the same point: deeper, meaning-based processing lasts longer.

slides.question: Which kind of rehearsal produces the most effective long-term encoding?
options: Elaborative rehearsal linking new and old knowledge
slides.why: Making connections between new and known information builds more retrieval routes. Rote repetition works, but less well.

slides.heading: Learning the cranial nerves
slides.story: Kemi repeats the twelve cranial nerves fifty times and forgets them by Friday. Her friend Ali links each nerve to its job and to a patient they saw on a clinic visit: the facial nerve to a man whose smile drooped on one side. Weeks later, Ali still remembers; the links pull each name back.
slides.takeaway: Association rehearsal ties new facts to existing knowledge, so they are easier to retrieve later.

slides.heading: Organisation helps
slides.body:
Material presented in an **organised** way, for example grouped into categories, is remembered better than the same items in random order.

**Bousfield (1953)** showed something more striking: when people heard words in a **random** order (animals, names, vegetables, professions mixed together), they tended to recall them **grouped by category**. They rearranged the list in their minds.

terms.meaning: Putting information into memory in a usable form
Linking new information to what one already knows
Grouping randomly presented items into categories during recall
Imposing one's own structure on unrelated items

slides.question: Bousfield (1953) found that people given a randomly ordered word list tended to:
options: Recall words in the exact order heard
slides.why: People spontaneously regrouped items into categories, which is clustering.

slides.heading: The market list
slides.story: Mama Tunde's shopping list reads: tomatoes, soap, crayfish, matches, pepper, toothpaste, onions. At the market, she recalls it as 'soup things: tomatoes, pepper, onions, crayfish; house things: soap, toothpaste, matches'. Nobody taught her to; her mind grouped the items itself.
slides.takeaway: Clustering imposes our own categories on a random list, making it easier to recall.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'describe encoding through association and organisation'. Show the rehearsal continuum, then organisation and clustering with Bousfield (1953). Objectives use scenarios: someone grouping items or linking new facts to old ones. The trap: calling clustering 'chunking'. Chunking groups items for short-term memory span; clustering groups them by category in recall.
slides.sampleQuestion: When randomly presented items are recalled grouped into categories, this is known as: (a) chunking (b) clustering (c) rote rehearsal (d) dual coding
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b): clustering (Bousfield, 1953). In essays, contrast it with rote rehearsal and explain why organisation aids retrieval.

points: Memories are filed under many associations; more links mean easier recall.
We store highlights, not every detail.
Rehearsal runs from rote repetition to rich association.
Organised material is easier to remember than random material.
Clustering: we regroup random items into categories (Bousfield, 1953).

questions.stem: The more associations a piece of information has in memory, the:
questions.explanation: Each association is another route to the memory, so retrieval becomes easier.

questions.stem: Simple repetition of information is called:
questions.explanation: Rote rehearsal is plain repetition. Elaborative rehearsal links new and old information.

questions.stem: Grouping randomly presented items into categories during recall is called:
questions.explanation: Clustering is the regrouping of random items by category, shown by Bousfield (1953).

questions.stem: Long-term memory is often likened to a library catalogue because:
options: Memories are filed under many index points
questions.explanation: Like a catalogue, memory files each item under several cues that can lead to it.

questions.stem: Material is easier to remember when it is presented:
options: In an organised way, by category
questions.explanation: Organisation by category aids memory compared with random presentation.

questions.stem: Why do we not remember every word spoken during a long event?
options: Memory stores highlights, not every detail
questions.explanation: Encoding is selective; we keep the gist and key moments.

questions.stem: To learn 'osmosis', Chidi links it to how garri swells when soaked in water. He is using:
questions.explanation: Linking new information to something already known is association (elaborative) rehearsal.

questions.stem: Students hear the words 'goat, Tunde, carrot, nurse, cow, Ada, yam, teacher' in that order. Many recall 'goat, cow; Tunde, Ada; carrot, yam; nurse, teacher'. This demonstrates:
questions.explanation: Recalling random items regrouped into categories is clustering.

questions.stem: A student who repeats a definition 30 times but cannot apply it a week later most likely relied on:
questions.explanation: Rote rehearsal creates weaker, less connected traces than elaboration.

questions.stem: Clustering differs from chunking because clustering:
options: Is regrouping by category during recall from long-term memory
Is the same as rote rehearsal
questions.explanation: Chunking packs items into units to stretch short-term span; clustering reorganises items by category in recall.

questions.stem: The idea that rehearsal is a continuum means:
options: Rehearsal ranges from simple repetition to rich association
questions.explanation: Rehearsal varies in depth, from rote at one end to elaborate association at the other.

questions.stem: All of the following improve long-term encoding EXCEPT:
options: Presenting items in a jumbled, unrelated way
Relating new information to known information
questions.explanation: Jumbled presentation makes encoding harder; the other three are recognised good techniques.

questions.stem: I. Rote rehearsal cannot get information into long-term memory. II. Elaborate rehearsal produces more effective encoding. III. People impose their own organisation on unrelated items. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: II and III are correct. I is false: rote rehearsal can get information into long-term memory, just less effectively.

questions.stem: A researcher finds that people recall a random word list in category groups even when told nothing about categories. This most strongly suggests that:
options: Memory stores items in the order heard
People actively organise material during encoding and retrieval
questions.explanation: Spontaneous clustering shows memory is an active organiser, not a passive recorder.

questions.stem: Which study habit best combines association and organisation?
options: Copying the textbook word for word
Building a concept map linking topics to known examples
questions.explanation: A concept map organises material into structure and links it to existing knowledge, using both principles.

sections.name: Tip of the tongue and dual coding

lesson.title: Sound, meaning and pictures
lesson.hook: You meet someone at a wedding. You know their name starts with 'Ti', has three syllables, and is definitely not Tiwalade. How can you know so much about a word you cannot find?

slides.heading: The tip-of-the-tongue state
slides.body:
A **tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state** happens when you **cannot recall** a word or name but **know something about it**: its first letter, its length, what it sounds like.

Sometimes the word arrives in seconds, sometimes hours later, and sometimes never. Often a related cue, like picturing where you met the person, suddenly unlocks it.

slides.heading: The classic TOT study
slides.body:
**Brown and McNeill (1966)** read definitions of uncommon words to students, such as *nepotism* or *sampan*, and asked for the word. Their 56 students produced **360 TOT states**.

One definition described a navigation instrument for measuring the angle of the sun, moon and stars at sea. Students in a TOT state offered words similar in **meaning** (*astrolabe, compass*) or in **sound** (*secant, sextet*). The target was *sextant*.

slides.heading: What TOT reveals
slides.body:
In TOT states that were later resolved, about **half** of the guesses had the **same number of syllables** as the target, and over half had the correct **first letter**. Many guessed the right prefix or suffix.

The lesson: words are encoded not only by **meaning** but also by **sound and form**. We can retrieve a word through what it sounds or looks like, not just what it means.

slides.question: Brown and McNeill's TOT findings suggest that words are stored in long-term memory by:
options: Both meaning and sound or form
slides.why: People's near-misses matched the target either in meaning or in sound, syllables and first letter, so both codes are used.

slides.heading: The dual-coding hypothesis
slides.body:
**Allan Paivio** proposed that memory uses **two systems**: a **verbal** system for words and a **non-verbal (imagery)** system for pictures.

We tend to use **imagery** for **concrete objects and events** (a mango, a danfo) and **words** for **abstract ideas and language** (justice, theory). The two systems are **independent but interconnected**: either can be used alone, but they pass information back and forth.

slides.heading: Mango versus democracy
slides.story: Asked to remember 'mango' and 'democracy', Ruth instantly pictures a ripe yellow mango and also stores the word. For 'democracy', no clear picture comes, so she relies on the word alone. A week later, she recalls 'mango' easily; 'democracy' takes longer.
slides.takeaway: Concrete words can be stored in both codes, giving two routes back; abstract words often rely on one.

slides.heading: Why two codes beat one
slides.body:
If an item is stored **both** as a word and as an image, there are **two routes** to retrieve it. This explains why **concrete** words are usually remembered better than abstract ones, and why pictures are often better recalled than words.

There is still **debate** about how much, and what kind of, material each system holds.

slides.question: According to dual-coding theory, imagery is mainly used for:
slides.why: Imagery suits concrete objects and events; words handle ideas and language.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Dual coding is often a fill-in-the-gap: imagery for ___, words for ___. Know that the systems are independent but interconnected, not separate and isolated. TOT questions test what near-misses reveal: same first letter, same syllables, similar sound or meaning. The trap: saying TOT shows words are stored by meaning alone.
slides.sampleQuestion: According to the dual-coding hypothesis, the verbal and imagery systems are: (a) identical (b) independent but interconnected (c) completely isolated (d) used only in childhood
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). In an essay, define both systems, say which kinds of material each handles, and explain why concrete words are remembered better.

points: TOT: you cannot recall a word but know features of it.
Brown and McNeill (1966): near-misses match in sound or meaning.
Words are encoded by meaning and by sound and form.
Dual coding (Paivio): verbal and imagery systems.
Imagery for concrete things, words for abstract ideas; two codes, two routes.

questions.stem: The tip-of-the-tongue state is when a person:
options: Cannot recall a word but knows something about it
questions.explanation: TOT is partial retrieval: the word is missing, but features like its first letter are available.

questions.stem: The dual-coding hypothesis is associated with:
questions.explanation: Allan Paivio proposed dual coding. Bousfield is linked with clustering.

questions.stem: According to dual coding, the two memory systems are:
questions.explanation: Paivio's two codes are a verbal system and a non-verbal imagery system.

questions.stem: In Brown and McNeill's study, students in TOT states often guessed words that:
options: Had nothing in common with the target
Were similar in sound or meaning to the target
questions.explanation: Near-misses matched the target in meaning or in sound, showing partial access.

questions.stem: In dual-coding theory, words are mainly used for:
questions.explanation: The verbal code handles abstract ideas and language; imagery handles concrete objects.

questions.stem: The verbal and imagery systems in dual-coding theory are described as:
questions.explanation: Each can work alone, but they exchange information.

questions.stem: Trying to recall 'sextant', a student says 'sexton'. This near-miss is based on:
questions.explanation: 'Sexton' sounds like 'sextant' but means something unrelated, so it is a sound-based guess.

questions.stem: Another student, trying for 'sextant', says 'compass'. This near-miss is based on:
questions.explanation: A compass is a similar navigation tool, so the guess is related in meaning.

questions.stem: Students remember 'elephant' better than 'freedom' in a word list. Dual-coding theory explains this because 'elephant':
options: Can be stored as both a word and an image
questions.explanation: Concrete words get an image code as well as a verbal code, giving two retrieval routes.

questions.stem: TOT research shows all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Words are encoded by meaning only
People often know the number of syllables
People often know the first letter of the missing word
Retrieval can use sound or form
questions.explanation: TOT findings show words are encoded by sound and form as well as meaning, so 'meaning only' is wrong.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Brown and McNeill (1966) studied TOT states. Paivio proposed dual coding; Bousfield studied clustering.

questions.stem: Why are pictures often recalled better than words, according to dual coding?
options: Pictures are encoded both as images and as verbal labels
questions.explanation: People usually name pictures as well as see them, so they get two codes.

questions.stem: I. Imagery handles concrete objects and events. II. The two codes cannot exchange information. III. There is debate about how much each system stores. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. II is false: the systems are interconnected and transfer information.

questions.stem: A person in a TOT state recalls the target only after picturing where they met the speaker. This best shows that:
options: A related cue can unlock a word that is stored but temporarily inaccessible
questions.explanation: The word was available but not accessible until a related cue opened a route to it.

questions.stem: A lecturer wants students to remember abstract terms better. Using dual-coding theory, the best advice is to:
options: Link each term to a concrete image or example
questions.explanation: Adding a concrete image gives abstract terms a second, imagery code and another retrieval route.
